name: Alan Macfarlane
specialization: Quantitative methods in witchcraft history; Essex county study; guilt/charity-refused mechanism

major_works.title: Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England
major_works.significance: First major quantitative study of English witchcraft using county records; developed guilt-projection mechanism and pioneered database methods in witchcraft history

major_works.title: The Origins of English Individualism
major_works.significance: Broader social history framework arguing for early English individualism; contextualizes witchcraft within changing community structures

core_argument: English witchcraft accusations were generated by the guilt-projection mechanism: as community bonds weakened under early capitalism and individualism, householders who refused charity to poor neighbors and subsequently suffered misfortune projected guilt onto the refused neighbor as a witch. The 'crime' of witchcraft was effectively a crime of accusation, driven by the accuser's psychological need.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Essex assize and quarter sessions records, church court records, county-level trial documentation from 1560-1680
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Social characteristics of accusers and accused; timing and pattern of accusations; community economic relationships
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Quantitative statistical analysis of trial records; social anthropological comparison with African witchcraft beliefs (Evans-Pritchard)
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Community-level: social-structural changes enabling guilt projection

key_contributions.claim: Accusers typically were wealthier than accused; they had refused charity and felt guilty; subsequent misfortune was attributed to the beggar's curse
key_contributions.implication: Witchcraft accusation was psychologically driven by the accuser, not evidence of the accused's malice

key_contributions.claim: Statistical analysis of county-level records can reveal structural patterns invisible in individual case studies
key_contributions.implication: Established a methodological template for database-driven witchcraft history (later developed by Goodare's Scottish survey)

key_contributions.claim: Evans-Pritchard's analysis of Azande witchcraft provides analytical models applicable to European historical cases
key_contributions.implication: Social anthropology and history can productively collaborate on witchcraft analysis

reception_and_critique.major_influences: E.E. Evans-Pritchard (social anthropology of witchcraft), Keith Thomas, quantitative social history methods
criticisms: Charity-refused thesis critiqued as too schematic; cases do not always fit the pattern
Essex focus may not generalize beyond England
Insufficient attention to gender as explanatory factor
Anthropological comparison with Azande seen as potentially misleading by some historians

historiographical_significance: Macfarlane's Essex study pioneered quantitative methods in witchcraft history and established the guilt-projection mechanism as a major explanatory framework. Working alongside Keith Thomas, he helped define the social history approach to English witchcraft that dominated the field for a generation. His database methodology directly influenced later digital humanities approaches to witchcraft records.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
